## Chapter 103: Graphs and Quality Tools in Minitab

### The Graph Menu

The Graph menu sits in Minitab's top menu bar. Within it, you have access to more than 20 graphical analysis options — with more detailed options for each chart type. We won't cover every chart type, but you can use your own data to explore the ones we don't cover.

If you want to explore the graph options along with the steps presented in this chapter, start by copying the information below into a new Minitab worksheet. Make sure both columns are flagged by Minitab as containing numbers (that is, no "T" designation in the column header).

*(Two example data columns: C1 with values 1 to 5 repeated twice, and C2 with decimal values between 1.4 and 6.2, used for the scatter, histogram and other chart examples in this chapter.)*

### Scatter Plot

Scatter plots plot each data point on X-Y axes and can help teams see how two inputs or data elements might be related. Scatter plots are often the first step in a regression analysis, because they let you quickly check whether correlation is plausible.

To create a scatter plot using the data above, select Graph > Scatterplots > Simple and click OK.

Click the first row under Y-variables and select column C2. Click the first row under X-variables and select column C1.

<figure class="figure2026">
<div style="background:#eef4f6;border:1px solid #cedde1;border-radius:8px;padding:16px;max-width:348px;margin:0.6rem auto;">
<svg aria-label="Scatterplot dialog box in Minitab" role="img" style="width:100%;height:auto;display:block;" viewBox="0 0 300 158" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
<rect fill="#f8fbfb" height="138" stroke="#cedde1" width="280" x="10" y="10"></rect><rect fill="#00688f" height="28" rx="4" width="280" x="10" y="10"></rect><text fill="#f8fbfb" font-family="Segoe UI, sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="700" x="22" y="29">Scatterplot: Simple</text><text fill="#52646b" font-family="Segoe UI, sans-serif" font-size="12" x="24" y="50">Y variables</text><rect fill="#f8fbfb" height="20" stroke="#cedde1" width="252" x="24" y="56"></rect><text fill="#132e3a" font-family="Consolas, monospace" font-size="11" x="30" y="71">C2</text><text fill="#52646b" font-family="Segoe UI, sans-serif" font-size="12" x="24" y="96">X variables</text><rect fill="#f8fbfb" height="20" stroke="#cedde1" width="252" x="24" y="102"></rect><text fill="#132e3a" font-family="Consolas, monospace" font-size="11" x="30" y="117">C1</text>
</svg>
</div>
<figcaption>Minitab: Graph &gt; Scatterplot &gt; Simple (or With Regression to include the fitted line).</figcaption>
</figure>

Click OK, and Minitab generates a scatter plot of the data. You can see that, for x = 1, the y values in our data range between 3 and 5. You can also see that there doesn't appear to be a relationship between the x and y values.

<img alt="Scatter diagram of C2 versus C1 generated by Minitab, showing points scattered with no apparent relationship between the variables" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />

Now, copy the data below into columns C4 and C5 in the same worksheet.

*(New data column C4 with values 1 to 5, and C5 with increasing correlated values, from 0.9 to 5.0.)*

Select Graph > Scatterplots > Simple. Change the x and y references so that x is C4 and y is C5. Click OK, and Minitab generates the chart below. This chart is different from the previous one — this data does appear to be correlated in some way.

<img alt="Scatter diagram of C5 versus C4 generated by Minitab, showing a clear positive linear correlation between the variables" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />

You can add a regression line to your scatter plot by selecting the "with regression" option in the Scatterplots dialog box.

If it wasn't obvious just from looking at the plotted points, the line makes it even more apparent that, as x increases, y increases. Remember, this doesn't necessarily mean that x causes y, but the two appear to be correlated. Upon seeing a result like this in a scatter plot, a Six Sigma practitioner might run a regression test to determine the probability of correlation between the two factors. Running that analysis in Minitab is covered in the next chapter.

If a correlation is observed during a statistical analysis, the statistical proof by itself (the math behind the conclusion) probably won't be much help in a presentation. As discussed in chapter 43, you may want to include illustrations of the statistical analysis, which is one more reason to use the scatter plot.

### Histogram

Throughout this book, we've worked with histograms several times. Histograms help Six Sigma practitioners understand the shape of the data, which also helps in understanding how the data is distributed. You can create histograms in Minitab by selecting Graph > Histogram.

<img alt="Scatter diagram of C5 versus C4 (repeated), showing the positive linear correlation between the variables" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />

Choose the "Simple" option for a histogram with no other elements. If you're following along, select column C2 from your worksheet in the graph variables box and click OK.

<figure class="figure2026">
<div style="background:#eef4f6;border:1px solid #cedde1;border-radius:8px;padding:16px;max-width:348px;margin:0.6rem auto;">
<svg aria-label="Histogram dialog box in Minitab" role="img" style="width:100%;height:auto;display:block;" viewBox="0 0 300 112" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
<rect fill="#f8fbfb" height="92" stroke="#cedde1" width="280" x="10" y="10"></rect><rect fill="#00688f" height="28" rx="4" width="280" x="10" y="10"></rect><text fill="#f8fbfb" font-family="Segoe UI, sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="700" x="22" y="29">Histogram: Simple</text><text fill="#52646b" font-family="Segoe UI, sans-serif" font-size="12" x="24" y="50">Graph variables</text><rect fill="#f8fbfb" height="20" stroke="#cedde1" width="252" x="24" y="56"></rect><text fill="#132e3a" font-family="Consolas, monospace" font-size="11" x="30" y="71">C2</text>
</svg>
</div>
<figcaption>Minitab: Graph &gt; Histogram &gt; Simple (or With Fit to overlay the fitted normal curve).</figcaption>
</figure>

Minitab creates a histogram of the data in column C2. That column has only 20 data points, which can make it hard to tell whether the data is normally distributed from a graphical analysis alone. Recall the lessons on sample size and the Central Limit Theorem. Smaller samples don't always provide enough data to draw analytical conclusions, but as the size of the dataset grows, most data approaches the normal curve.

<img alt="Histogram of C2 generated by Minitab (simple version, no fitted curve)" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />

Sometimes, placing a fitted curve over your data can help give a better sense of its shape. Recreate the histogram of the data in column C2, but select "with fit" in the Histograms dialog box.

Minitab fits a normal curve over the histogram to help visualize the distribution of your data. In this case, we might be tempted to say the data is somewhat normal. Only the very tall column in the center throws off the overall symmetry of the chart. Even so, there isn't enough information here to draw a conclusion.

<img alt="Histogram of C2 with fitted normal curve, Mean 3,796, StDev 1,337, N=20" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />

Create a histogram with a fitted curve for the data in column C1.

The result is obviously a uniform distribution of the data, which doesn't fit the normal curve. In this case, you can state with more confidence that the data is not normal.

<img alt="Histogram of C1 with fitted normal curve, showing bars of nearly equal height (uniform distribution) that don't follow the normal curve" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />

Here's the graphical summary for the data in column C2, so we can confirm our conclusions about normality once again. Remember, that summary is found under Stat > Basic Statistics > Graphical Summary.

<img alt="Summary Report generated by Minitab for the C2 data: histogram with fitted curve, boxplot, descriptive statistics (Mean 3,7850, StDev 1,3406), and Anderson-Darling normality test (P-Value 0,909)" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />

The p-value for the Anderson-Darling normality test lets us fail to reject the null hypothesis that the data is normal. The rest of the information in this summary also tends to point toward a conclusion of normality. As you can see, the graphical summary provides the same information as the histogram chart, plus the extra information that lets Six Sigma practitioners make a better decision about the distribution of the data. For that reason, you're more likely to run the graphical analysis for an overall understanding of your data. The histogram function is still valuable for analyzing certain specific information or for generating a single chart you want to include in a presentation or report.

### Dotplot

A dotplot is similar to a histogram in helping you understand the shape of the data, but it plots individual data points along a single line.

Access the dotplot function under Graph > Dotplot.

In the example dotplot chart below, you can see that four data points measure as 9; three data points measure as 5, 6, 7 and 8. Each measurement above 10 has only one data point associated with it. The simple dotplot shown below is usually used for smaller sample sizes, and teams may even create quick dotplot sketches on whiteboards or paper during a meeting if they want a quick visual representation of the data for discussion.

<img alt="Example dotplot of column C7, showing data points spread along a number line from 1 to 19, with points concentrated around the value 9" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />

The dotplots created above are simple dotplots. They represent a single Y (one measurement, one dataset) along a single line. You can also represent measurements of a single Y with groups, separated or stacked. The concept is similar to a stacked bar chart, in which you break down the measurements by another variable or factor. For example, you might be creating a dotplot of the amount of work done per hour. If you have all the numbers per person logged during a shift, you could group the information by person.

<img alt="Dotplot of column C7 grouped by person (C9: Sue, Mary, Mark, John, Ed, Anita), with a different symbol for each operator along the number line" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />

You can also work with more than one measurement, or Y, with simple, stacked, or grouped data. For example, you might have data from two shifts with employees on each shift.

The dotplot below shows the amount of work done each hour by two employees on each shift. You can immediately see that shift 2 employees appear to be producing more per hour than shift 1 employees — there are more data points located above the higher numbers on the second shift's chart.

<img alt="Dotplot with multiple Ys stacked by shift, comparing "Shift 1D" and "Shift 2d"" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />

To select the type of dotplot you want to create, click the appropriate image in the Dotplots box.

Select the appropriate columns for your dotplot data. The graph variables are always your data columns. The categorical variables for grouping are the columns with your categories listed, such as people's names, shift labels, or time. If you're working with multiple Ys, you can select more than one data column in the graph variables box.

<div style="background:#eef4f6;border:1px solid #cedde1;border-radius:8px;padding:16px;max-width:348px;margin:0.6rem auto;">

### Boxplot

In chapter 44, you learned how to create boxplots in Excel. Minitab creates box-and-whisker plots without all the editing you'd need to do in Excel. As with dotplots, you can also create boxplots with single datasets, groups of data, and data subgroups.

*(Example data table with three groups — Group A, Group B, Group C — each with about 15 values between 3 and 19, including an outlier of 18 in Group A, used for the boxplot examples below.)*

Copy the data above into Minitab to create some boxplots.

Select Graph > Boxplot > One Y Simple.

Select "Group A" in the Graph Variables box.

<figure class="figure2026">
<div style="background:#eef4f6;border:1px solid #cedde1;border-radius:8px;padding:16px;max-width:348px;margin:0.6rem auto;">
<svg aria-label="Boxplot dialog box in Minitab" role="img" style="width:100%;height:auto;display:block;" viewBox="0 0 300 112" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
<rect fill="#f8fbfb" height="92" stroke="#cedde1" width="280" x="10" y="10"></rect><rect fill="#00688f" height="28" rx="4" width="280" x="10" y="10"></rect><text fill="#f8fbfb" font-family="Segoe UI, sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="700" x="22" y="29">Boxplot: One Y, Simple</text><text fill="#52646b" font-family="Segoe UI, sans-serif" font-size="12" x="24" y="50">Graph variables</text><rect fill="#f8fbfb" height="20" stroke="#cedde1" width="252" x="24" y="56"></rect><text fill="#132e3a" font-family="Consolas, monospace" font-size="11" x="30" y="71">Group A</text>
</svg>
</div>
<figcaption>Minitab: Graph &gt; Boxplot &gt; One Y, Simple (or With Groups, specifying the grouping categorical column).</figcaption>
</figure>

Click OK.

Minitab returns the boxplot of the data above. We can see that the data has a mean of approximately 5 and that there is an outlier around 18 in the data. The outlier is indicated by the point at the top of the chart.

<img alt="Boxplot of Group A generated by Minitab, showing the box concentrated between 4 and 6 and an outlier flagged by an asterisk near 18" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />

If you wanted to compare all three groups of data, you could plot them all at once.

Select Graph > Boxplot > Multiple Ys Simple.

Select all three data columns in the Graph Variables box.

Click OK.

The chart above provides more information than a single boxplot for group A. You can see there are outliers in each data group. You can also see that the mean of each group is progressively higher — the mean is indicated by the line at the center of each box. The boxes are roughly the same size, indicating that the standard deviation, or variance, within each dataset is roughly the same.

<img alt="Boxplot comparing Group A, Group B, and Group C generated by Minitab, showing progressively higher means and outliers in each group" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />

What would happen if your data were organized differently from the table above, which has three separate groups of data? What if you had two columns of data, with the first column being the group indicator and the second column the measurement? The data for two groups might look like the table below.

*(Example data table with two columns — Group (1 or 2) and Result — totaling about 40 rows, including a few outliers such as 18, 14 and 12, used for the next boxplot example with a categorical variable.)*

To create a boxplot for this type of data, select Graph > Boxplot > One Y with Groups.

Select the Result column in the Graph Variables box. Select the Group column in the Categorical Variables box. Note that you can only plot up to 4 categorical variables at once.

Click OK.

Minitab returns the boxplot below. It's similar to the boxplot returned for the three subgroups, although obviously there are only two groups here, because there were only two different categories listed in our data table.

<img alt="Boxplot of Result grouped by Group (1 and 2) generated by Minitab, with outliers flagged in both groups" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />

### Interval Plot

Interval plots are useful when you want to analyze the means or the variance within a single dataset or across data subgroups. Creating interval plots in Minitab essentially follows the same steps as creating boxplots, and you can split interval plots into the same groups.

Using the first data table from the boxplot section above, in Minitab select Graph > Interval Plot > Multiple Ys Simple. Select all three data columns in the Graph Variables box. Click OK.

Minitab returns the interval plots below.

<img alt="Interval Plot of Group A, Group B, and Group C generated by Minitab, with 95% confidence intervals for the mean of each group" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />

Just as with the similar boxplot, you can see that the mean of each group is slightly higher than the one before it. You can also see that the spread of the data is roughly the same for each group. What interval plots don't show are the outliers.

You can create interval plots for all the data used in the boxplot examples, exactly as you created the boxplots. The only difference is that you select interval plots from the Graph menu.

### Bar Chart

Excel is a great tool for creating colorful, presentable bar and pie charts, but you can also quickly create these charts in Minitab for analysis purposes. Use the phone-calls-per-hour data below to create a bar chart in Minitab.

*(Data table: number of phone calls logged each hour, from 8:00 to 21:00, ranging between 57 and 198 calls.)*

Select Graph > Bar Chart. From the "bars represent" dropdown, choose "values from a table." Select Simple under "one column of values." Click OK.

<figure class="figure2026">
<div style="background:#eef4f6;border:1px solid #cedde1;border-radius:8px;padding:16px;max-width:348px;margin:0.6rem auto;">
<svg aria-label="Bar Chart dialog box in Minitab" role="img" style="width:100%;height:auto;display:block;" viewBox="0 0 300 158" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
<rect fill="#f8fbfb" height="138" stroke="#cedde1" width="280" x="10" y="10"></rect><rect fill="#00688f" height="28" rx="4" width="280" x="10" y="10"></rect><text fill="#f8fbfb" font-family="Segoe UI, sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="700" x="22" y="29">Bar Chart: Values from a table</text><text fill="#52646b" font-family="Segoe UI, sans-serif" font-size="12" x="24" y="50">Graph variables</text><rect fill="#f8fbfb" height="20" stroke="#cedde1" width="252" x="24" y="56"></rect><text fill="#132e3a" font-family="Consolas, monospace" font-size="11" x="30" y="71">Phone calls</text><text fill="#52646b" font-family="Segoe UI, sans-serif" font-size="12" x="24" y="96">Categorical variable</text><rect fill="#f8fbfb" height="20" stroke="#cedde1" width="252" x="24" y="102"></rect><text fill="#132e3a" font-family="Consolas, monospace" font-size="11" x="30" y="117">Hour</text>
</svg>
</div>
<figcaption>Minitab: Graph &gt; Bar Chart &gt; Values from a table, One column of values, Simple.</figcaption>
</figure>

In the Bar Chart dialog box, select the "phone calls" column in the graph variables box. That's always where you select the column containing the data to be plotted. Select the "hour" column in the categorical variables box. That's always where you select the information you want displayed along the x-axis.

Minitab returns a simple bar chart, as shown below.

<img alt="Bar chart "Chart of Phone calls" generated by Minitab, showing the number of calls per hour, peaking at 7pm (198 calls) and lowest at 9pm (57 calls)" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />

The options for creating bar charts in Minitab are similar to Excel's: you can create stacked or clustered bar charts. But you can also create charts from data without having to perform the same calculations you might need to do in Excel. For example, if you select "Counts of unique values" from the bar chart box's dropdown, Minitab will count the unique values for you. Try this with the data table below, which lists the number of errors in 13 work samples.

Select Graph > Bar Chart. Select "Counts of unique values" in the Bars Represent dropdown box. Select Simple and click OK.

Minitab counts the number of times each unique value — 1, 2, 3 or 4 — appears in the data and creates a bar chart of those counts.

<img alt="Bar chart "Chart of Number of Errors" generated by Minitab, showing the count of samples with 1, 2, 3, or 4 errors (6, 3, 2, and 2 samples, respectively)" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />

Minitab also offers a few options for ordering the data in your chart. Recreate the first calls-per-hour chart again, but in the Bar Chart dialog box, click "Chart Options" and choose to sort by decreasing Y.

<figure class="figure2026">
<div style="background:#eef4f6;border:1px solid #cedde1;border-radius:8px;padding:16px;max-width:348px;margin:0.6rem auto;">
<svg aria-label="Category sorting options in Minitab" role="img" style="width:100%;height:auto;display:block;" viewBox="0 0 300 112" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
<rect fill="#f8fbfb" height="92" stroke="#cedde1" width="280" x="10" y="10"></rect><rect fill="#00688f" height="28" rx="4" width="280" x="10" y="10"></rect><text fill="#f8fbfb" font-family="Segoe UI, sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="700" x="22" y="29">Chart Options — ordenação</text><text fill="#52646b" font-family="Segoe UI, sans-serif" font-size="12" x="24" y="50">Order Main X Groups By</text><rect fill="#f8fbfb" height="20" stroke="#cedde1" width="252" x="24" y="56"></rect><text fill="#132e3a" font-family="Consolas, monospace" font-size="11" x="30" y="71">Decreasing Y</text>
</svg>
</div>
<figcaption>Minitab: in the chart dialog, the Chart Options button (or Pie Options for a pie chart) lets you sort categories by value.</figcaption>
</figure>

Click OK. Click OK again.

Minitab places the x-axis data in order from highest to lowest — much as you'd see in a Pareto chart. This is useful for anyone conducting an analysis, because it gives a sense of the highest and lowest values in a dataset. Minitab also lets you sort the other way, show the information as a percentage of the total, or accumulate the totals along the x-axis.

<img alt="Bar chart "Chart of Phone calls" generated by Minitab, now sorted from the highest to the lowest number of calls (descending, from 7pm to 9pm)" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />

### Pie Chart

Pie charts in Minitab follow steps similar to bar charts. To create a pie chart, copy the data from the table below into Minitab.

*(Data table: ten process steps, A through J, with the duration in minutes of each, ranging between 3 and 64 minutes.)*

Select Graph > Pie Chart. Click the option to plot values from a table. Select "Process Step" as the categorical variable and "Minutes" as the summary variable.

<figure class="figure2026">
<div style="background:#eef4f6;border:1px solid #cedde1;border-radius:8px;padding:16px;max-width:348px;margin:0.6rem auto;">
<svg aria-label="Pie Chart dialog box in Minitab" role="img" style="width:100%;height:auto;display:block;" viewBox="0 0 300 184" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">

</svg>

<figcaption>Minitab: Graph &gt; Pie Chart. Use 'Chart values from a table' for already summarized data, or 'Chart counts of unique values' to count occurrences by category.</figcaption>
</figure>

Click OK. Minitab returns the pie chart below.

<img alt="Pie chart "Pie Chart of Process Step" generated by Minitab, with ten colored slices corresponding to process steps A through J" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />

Just as with bar charts, you can choose to plot counts of unique values. Use the error-count data from the bar chart example to create a pie chart of counts of unique values.

Select Graph > Pie Chart. Select the option to plot counts of unique variables. Select "Number of Errors" as the categorical variable.

Click OK.

Just as in the bar chart example, Minitab counts the number of times each unique value occurs in the data and presents it as a pie chart.

<img alt="Pie chart "Pie Chart of Number of Errors" generated by Minitab, with four slices corresponding to categories 1, 2, 3, and 4" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />

Also similar to the bar chart, you can have Minitab sort the data in your pie chart. Recreate the pie chart from the first example in this section, which showed the number of errors at each process step.

Select Graph → Pie Chart, "Chart values from a table," with "Process Step" as the categorical variable and "Minutes" as the summary variable. Just as with the bar chart, the Pie Options button lets you reorder the slices (for example, "Order Slices By: Increasing volume").

Click OK. Click OK again.

Minitab returns a pie chart with the data ordered from smallest to largest, clockwise around the pie. Compared to the first pie chart of this data, this one is probably easier to read and draw conclusions from, because it's easier to compare the size of each slice when they're ordered.

<img alt="Pie chart "Pie Chart of Process Step" generated by Minitab, now sorted from smallest to largest, clockwise, starting at G and ending at D" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />

### The Stat Menu: Quality Tools

Not all of Minitab's charts live in the Graph menu. You'll find control charts, run charts, and Pareto charts under the Stat menu. Creating control charts in Minitab was covered in PART V.

### Run Chart

Recall that a run chart is a graphical representation of data elements over time. In Minitab, you can also create a run chart of subgroup means or medians over time. Create run charts using the data table below, which represents the production time of several samples collected during specific hours of a shift. The quality team collects five samples per hour.

*(Data table: five production-time samples per hour, over 5 hours — 25 values total, ranging between 7 and 19.)*

In Minitab, select Stat > Quality Tools > Run Chart. The data is organized in a single column, where "production time" is the data to be plotted. Since the quality team collects 5 samples per hour, the subgroup size is 5.

<figure class="figure2026">
<div style="background:#eef4f6;border:1px solid #cedde1;border-radius:8px;padding:16px;max-width:348px;margin:0.6rem auto;">
<svg aria-label="Run Chart dialog box in Minitab" role="img" style="width:100%;height:auto;display:block;" viewBox="0 0 300 158" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
<rect fill="#f8fbfb" height="138" stroke="#cedde1" width="280" x="10" y="10"></rect><rect fill="#00688f" height="28" rx="4" width="280" x="10" y="10"></rect><text fill="#f8fbfb" font-family="Segoe UI, sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="700" x="22" y="29">Run Chart</text><text fill="#52646b" font-family="Segoe UI, sans-serif" font-size="12" x="24" y="50">Single column</text><rect fill="#f8fbfb" height="20" stroke="#cedde1" width="252" x="24" y="56"></rect><text fill="#132e3a" font-family="Consolas, monospace" font-size="11" x="30" y="71">Production Time</text><text fill="#52646b" font-family="Segoe UI, sans-serif" font-size="12" x="24" y="96">Subgroup size</text><rect fill="#f8fbfb" height="20" stroke="#cedde1" width="252" x="24" y="102"></rect><text fill="#132e3a" font-family="Consolas, monospace" font-size="11" x="30" y="117">5</text>
</svg>
</div>
<figcaption>Minitab: Stat &gt; Quality Tools &gt; Run Chart. Use 'Subgroups across rows' when each row already represents a subgroup rather than a single column.</figcaption>
</figure>

Click OK.

Plotted this way, Minitab plots the points for each subgroup on the chart in gray and then plots the mean in blue. The run line shown is for the mean of each subgroup. You can see that hours 1, 2 and 4 have roughly equal means, and hours 3 and 5 have lower means.

<img alt="Run Chart of Production Time generated by Minitab (subgroup/sample means), with statistics on the number of runs above and below the median" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />

Alternatively, you can plot all of your data points on a single run chart.

In Minitab, select Stat > Quality Tools > Run Chart. Select "subgroups across rows of." Select the production-time column in the box.

Click OK.

Minitab returns a simple run chart of your data.

<img alt="Run Chart of Production Time generated by Minitab (all 25 individual observations), with statistics on the number of runs above and below the median" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />

### Pareto Chart

In chapter 36, we covered how to create Pareto charts in Excel, but you'll recall that it required some data manipulation to put the chart in order, add trend lines, and create label percentages. In Excel, you needed totals, or summaries, of the data. In chapter 36, one of the Pareto charts created was about claim denials by payer, and the data was presented as totals in a table.

With Minitab, you don't need totals in a table. You can create a Pareto chart with more raw data. In the data table below, a quality team reviewed 150 denied claims to determine the reason for denial. You can copy and paste this data into Minitab, if you'd like, to create a Pareto chart.

*(Data table with 150 claims, each associated with a denial reason: Timely Filing, Missing Information, No Benefits, Lacking Medical Reason, Wrong Diagnosis Code, or Duplicate Claim.)*

Select Stat > Quality Tools > Pareto Chart. The defects or attributes being plotted are the claim denial reasons. There are no frequencies or variables by which this data is being grouped — you simply want to see how each type of denial impacts the total denial count. It's worth noting that this is one of the few times in Minitab where you can plot non-numeric data.

It's also important to note that Minitab will separate defects or attributes by unique values, and it differentiates by spelling, spacing, and capitalization. So "Timely Filing," "TimelyFiling," and "timely filing" would all be counted as separate attributes by the program. The Six Sigma practitioner needs to make sure the data is properly prepared and that all categorical descriptions match before running a Pareto chart. One way to do this is to prepare the data in Excel, where you can use find-and-replace to make sure all entries are corrected for spacing or spelling.

For this example, select "Do not combine," because there are only a few claim denial reasons in the data. If you have ten or more unique attributes, you can select the option to combine the remaining defects after 95 or 90 percent. The defects that make up the final 5 or 10 percent would be displayed in the Pareto chart as "other."

<figure class="figure2026">
<div style="background:#eef4f6;border:1px solid #cedde1;border-radius:8px;padding:16px;max-width:348px;margin:0.6rem auto;">
<svg aria-label="Pareto Chart dialog box in Minitab" role="img" style="width:100%;height:auto;display:block;" viewBox="0 0 300 158" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
<rect fill="#f8fbfb" height="138" stroke="#cedde1" width="280" x="10" y="10"></rect><rect fill="#00688f" height="28" rx="4" width="280" x="10" y="10"></rect><text fill="#f8fbfb" font-family="Segoe UI, sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="700" x="22" y="29">Pareto Chart</text><text fill="#52646b" font-family="Segoe UI, sans-serif" font-size="12" x="24" y="50">Defects or attribute data in</text><rect fill="#f8fbfb" height="20" stroke="#cedde1" width="252" x="24" y="56"></rect><text fill="#132e3a" font-family="Consolas, monospace" font-size="11" x="30" y="71">Claim Denial Reason</text><text fill="#52646b" font-family="Segoe UI, sans-serif" font-size="12" x="24" y="96">Combine remaining defects into one category after this %</text><rect fill="#f8fbfb" height="20" stroke="#cedde1" width="252" x="24" y="102"></rect><text fill="#132e3a" font-family="Consolas, monospace" font-size="11" x="30" y="117">Do not combine</text>
</svg>
</div>
<figcaption>Minitab: Stat &gt; Quality Tools &gt; Pareto Chart.</figcaption>
</figure>

Click OK.

<img alt="Pareto chart "Pareto Chart of Claim Denial Reason" generated by Minitab, with Duplicate Claim (57, 38,0%) as the largest reason, followed by Timely Filing, Lacking Medical Reason, No Benefits, Missing Information, and Wrong Diagnosis Code (6, 4,0%), with the cumulative-percentage line reaching 100%" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />

Minitab displays a Pareto chart with the bar chart, the cumulative percentage, and the detailed count. From this chart, you can quickly see that roughly 80 percent of the denied claims are caused by the top three denial reasons.

### Gage Studies

Another handy tool in Minitab is the ability to generate Gage R&R worksheets and interpret the results of a Gage R&R study. Gage R&R studies were covered earlier, in chapter 35, on the Measure phase.

Create a Gage R&R worksheet by selecting Stat > Quality Tools > Gage Study > Create Gage R&R Study Worksheet.

<figure class="figure2026">
<div style="background:#eef4f6;border:1px solid #cedde1;border-radius:8px;padding:16px;max-width:348px;margin:0.6rem auto;">
<svg aria-label="Create Gage R&amp;R Study Worksheet dialog box in Minitab" role="img" style="width:100%;height:auto;display:block;" viewBox="0 0 300 204" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
<rect fill="#f8fbfb" height="184" stroke="#cedde1" width="280" x="10" y="10"></rect><rect fill="#00688f" height="28" rx="4" width="280" x="10" y="10"></rect><text fill="#f8fbfb" font-family="Segoe UI, sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="700" x="22" y="29">Create Gage R&amp;R Study Worksheet</text><text fill="#52646b" font-family="Segoe UI, sans-serif" font-size="12" x="24" y="50">Number of parts</text><rect fill="#f8fbfb" height="20" stroke="#cedde1" width="252" x="24" y="56"></rect><text fill="#132e3a" font-family="Consolas, monospace" font-size="11" x="30" y="71">5</text><text fill="#52646b" font-family="Segoe UI, sans-serif" font-size="12" x="24" y="96">Number of operators</text><rect fill="#f8fbfb" height="20" stroke="#cedde1" width="252" x="24" y="102"></rect><text fill="#132e3a" font-family="Consolas, monospace" font-size="11" x="30" y="117">2 (Mike, Ann)</text><text fill="#52646b" font-family="Segoe UI, sans-serif" font-size="12" x="24" y="142">Number of replicates</text><rect fill="#f8fbfb" height="20" stroke="#cedde1" width="252" x="24" y="148"></rect><text fill="#132e3a" font-family="Consolas, monospace" font-size="11" x="30" y="163">2</text>
</svg>
</div>
<figcaption>Minitab: Stat &gt; Quality Tools &gt; Gage Study &gt; Create Gage R&amp;R Study Worksheet to generate the randomized measurement order.</figcaption>
</figure>

Minitab lets you enter a variety of information to set up a randomized Gage R&R study. In the example above, Mike and Ann are quality auditors reviewing dollies coming off a manufacturing line. In this study, each person will review five parts, and will do so twice.

Minitab lets you select the number of parts to be reviewed, the number of reviewers or operators, and the number of replicates — that is, how many times the review or measurement should be repeated. You can also click the blank space next to each part and operator number to name them, for clarity later on.

After setting up the dialog box as above, click OK.

Minitab generates a worksheet for the Gage R&R study. It randomizes how the parts are presented to each person, on each replicate. Recall from chapter 35: this is a critical step in a measurement analysis, because it helps reduce the chance that the operator remembers the measurement they recorded previously.

<img alt="Worksheet "Create Gage R&R Study Worksheet" generated by Minitab, with 20 rows in random order (RunOrder, Parts, Operators)" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:394px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />

Mike and Ann then take the measurements on each of the parts. In this case, they're measuring the parts in inches to make sure they fall within the required quality range. The Six Sigma practitioner running the Gage R&R isn't concerned with whether the parts fit within that range — they're concerned with whether the measurement system works. Can Ann and Mike repeat their measurements consistently, both within their own datasets and when compared against each other?

The measurements are collected and entered into Minitab.

<img alt="Minitab worksheet with the Measurement column filled in with the values measured by Mike and Ann for each part" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:355px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />

Since there's more than one operator and each is measuring every part, the Gage R&R Study (Crossed) option is chosen to analyze the measurement system — use "Crossed" whenever every operator measures every part (the most common case). Select "Parts" for the part numbers (even if the labels aren't numeric), the operators column, and the column with the measurements under "Measurement data."

<figure class="figure2026">
<div style="background:#eef4f6;border:1px solid #cedde1;border-radius:8px;padding:16px;max-width:348px;margin:0.6rem auto;">
<svg aria-label="Gage R&amp;R Study (Crossed) dialog box in Minitab" role="img" style="width:100%;height:auto;display:block;" viewBox="0 0 300 250" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
<rect fill="#f8fbfb" height="230" stroke="#cedde1" width="280" x="10" y="10"></rect><rect fill="#00688f" height="28" rx="4" width="280" x="10" y="10"></rect><text fill="#f8fbfb" font-family="Segoe UI, sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="700" x="22" y="29">Gage R&amp;R Study (Crossed)</text><text fill="#52646b" font-family="Segoe UI, sans-serif" font-size="12" x="24" y="50">Part numbers</text><rect fill="#f8fbfb" height="20" stroke="#cedde1" width="252" x="24" y="56"></rect><text fill="#132e3a" font-family="Consolas, monospace" font-size="11" x="30" y="71">Parts</text><text fill="#52646b" font-family="Segoe UI, sans-serif" font-size="12" x="24" y="96">Operators</text><rect fill="#f8fbfb" height="20" stroke="#cedde1" width="252" x="24" y="102"></rect><text fill="#132e3a" font-family="Consolas, monospace" font-size="11" x="30" y="117">Operators</text><text fill="#52646b" font-family="Segoe UI, sans-serif" font-size="12" x="24" y="142">Measurement data</text><rect fill="#f8fbfb" height="20" stroke="#cedde1" width="252" x="24" y="148"></rect><text fill="#132e3a" font-family="Consolas, monospace" font-size="11" x="30" y="163">C4</text><text fill="#52646b" font-family="Segoe UI, sans-serif" font-size="12" x="24" y="188">Method</text><rect fill="#f8fbfb" height="20" stroke="#cedde1" width="252" x="24" y="194"></rect><text fill="#132e3a" font-family="Consolas, monospace" font-size="11" x="30" y="209">ANOVA</text>
</svg>
</div>
<figcaption>Minitab: Stat &gt; Quality Tools &gt; Gage Study &gt; Gage R&amp;R Study (Crossed), metodo ANOVA.</figcaption>
</figure>

Minitab generates a series of graphical analyses to help determine whether the measurement system works. The two charts at the bottom show that each operator reproduces the other operator's results fairly closely. Each operator's Xbar chart looks almost identical, and the Parts * Operators Interaction chart is so close together that you can't even see Mike's blue square and line under Ann's red ones. The boxplot of the data also shows that each operator's information is very similar — the mean appears to be the same, as does the spread of the data.

The first chart details where the variation shows up in the measurements. For both Mike and Ann, the variation showed up when comparing the measurement of a part in the first round with the measurement of the same part in the second round. Even with that slight round-to-round variation, though, the overall variation is very small, and this Gage R&R indicates that the measurement system is working.

<img alt="Report "Gage R&R (ANOVA) Report for C4" generated by Minitab: six charts — Components of Variation (Gage R&R, Repeat, Reprod, Part-to-Part), R Chart by Operators, Xbar Chart by Operators, C4 by Parts, C4 by Operators, and Parts * Operators Interaction — showing that most of the variation comes from Part-to-Part and that Mike and Ann produce very similar results" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />
